section.title: The Twelve Memorial Stones
section.sectionRationale: The miracle at the Jordan is not to be forgotten. God commands that twelve men take twelve stones from the middle of the riverbed to build a memorial, so that future generations will ask what they mean and be told the story of what God did. The nation completes the crossing, Joshua is exalted before all Israel, and the stones are set up at Gilgal. It is one movement, the deliberate making of a memory that will preach God's power to children not yet born.
section.thesis: God cares that His mighty acts be remembered and retold, so He turns the crossing into a lasting sign: stones that will prompt a child's question and a parent's testimony, teaching every generation that the LORD's hand is mighty and calling all the earth, and all Israel, to fear Him.
section.frameNote: Four beats: the command to take twelve stones, verses 1 to 8; the completed crossing and Joshua's exaltation, verses 9 to 14; the priests come up and the river returns, verses 15 to 18; and the stones set up at Gilgal to teach the generations, verses 19 to 24.

units.label: The command to take twelve stones
units.note: when your children ask, what do these stones mean

verses.text: When the whole nation had finished crossing the Jordan, the LORD said to Joshua,
“Choose twelve men from among the people, one from each tribe,
and command them: ‘Take up for yourselves twelve stones from the middle of the Jordan where the priests were standing, carry them with you, and set them down in the place where you spend the night.’”
So Joshua summoned the twelve men he had appointed from the Israelites, one from each tribe,
and said to them, “Cross over before the ark of the LORD your God into the middle of the Jordan. Each of you is to take a stone upon his shoulder, according to the number of the tribes of Israel,
to serve as a sign among you. In the future, when your children ask, ‘What do these stones mean to you?’

you are to tell them, ‘The waters of the Jordan were cut off before the ark of the covenant of the LORD. When it crossed the Jordan, the waters were cut off.’ Therefore these stones will be a {{zikkaron|memorial}} to the Israelites forever.”

Thus the Israelites did as Joshua had commanded them. They took up twelve stones from the middle of the Jordan, one for each tribe of Israel, just as the LORD had told Joshua; and they carried them to the camp, where they set them down.

units.label: The completed crossing and Joshua's exaltation
units.note: the LORD exalted Joshua in the sight of all Israel

verses.text: Joshua also set up twelve stones in the middle of the Jordan, in the place where the priests who carried the ark of the covenant stood. And the stones are there to this day.

Now the priests who carried the ark remained standing in the middle of the Jordan until the people had completed everything the LORD had commanded Joshua to tell them, just as Moses had directed Joshua. The people hurried across,
and after everyone had finished crossing, the priests with the ark of the LORD crossed in the sight of the people.
The Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh crossed over before the Israelites, armed for battle as Moses had instructed them.
About 40,000 troops armed for battle crossed over before the LORD into the plains of Jericho.
On that day the LORD exalted Joshua in the sight of all Israel, and they revered him all the days of his life, just as they had revered Moses.

units.label: The priests come up and the river returns
units.note: the waters of the Jordan returned to their course

verses.text: Then the LORD said to Joshua,
“Command the priests who carry the ark of the Testimony to come up from the Jordan.”
So Joshua commanded the priests, “Come up from the Jordan.”

When the priests carrying the ark of the covenant of the LORD came up out of the Jordan and their feet touched the dry land, the waters of the Jordan returned to their course and overflowed all the banks as before.

units.label: The stones at Gilgal to teach the generations
units.note: so that all the peoples of the earth may know the hand of the LORD is mighty

verses.text: On the tenth day of the first month the people went up from the Jordan and camped at Gilgal on the eastern border of Jericho.
And there at Gilgal Joshua set up the twelve stones they had taken from the Jordan.
Then Joshua said to the Israelites, “In the future, when your children ask their fathers, ‘What is the meaning of these stones?’
you are to tell them, ‘Israel crossed the Jordan on dry ground.’
For the LORD your God dried up the waters of the Jordan before you until you had crossed over, just as He did to the Red Sea, which He dried up before us until we had crossed over.
He did this so that all the peoples of the earth may know that the {{yad|hand}} of the LORD is mighty, and so that you may always {{yare|fear}} the LORD your God.”

zikkaron.gloss: A memorial, remembrance, reminder. The twelve stones are a zikkaron, a permanent prompt to memory built into the landscape, so that God's saving act at the Jordan will not be forgotten but retold to every generation. The same idea shapes the Passover and, ultimately, the Lord's Supper, given so that His people would remember and proclaim what God has done.

yad.gloss: Hand, power, might. The purpose of the memorial is that all the peoples of the earth may know the yad of the LORD is mighty. The hand stands for God's active power; the crossing displays it, and the stones preserve the testimony to it, so that both the nations and Israel would reckon with the strong hand of God.

yare.gloss: To fear, reverence, stand in awe. The final aim of the whole sign is that Israel may always yare the LORD their God, a reverent awe that leads to trust and obedience. The remembering is not for its own sake; it is to keep alive the fear of the LORD, the fitting response to the God whose mighty hand they had just seen.

basic.context: As soon as the whole nation has crossed the Jordan, God gives an unusual command: build a memorial. Twelve men, one per tribe, are to carry twelve stones from the middle of the dried riverbed and set them up as a permanent marker. The point is memory. One day children will ask, what do these stones mean, and their parents will tell the story of how God stopped the river so Israel could cross. Joshua also sets up stones in the riverbed itself. The priests come up, the water returns, and the stones are finally erected at Gilgal. God says the purpose is that all the earth would know His mighty hand and that Israel would always fear Him. The question underneath is: how does faith get passed from one generation to the next?
basic.hermeneutics: This is historical narrative, and its clear teaching point is spelled out in the text itself: God's acts must be remembered and retold. The specific memorial of stones belongs to Israel's history, but the principle, deliberately building reminders and teaching children through them, is a lasting pattern God cares about deeply. The chapter also ties the Jordan crossing back to the Red Sea, reinforcing that this is a second exodus.
basic.originalLanguages: The stones are a zikkaron, a memorial, a built-in prompt to remembrance. Their purpose is that all the earth would know the yad, the hand, the mighty power of the LORD, and that Israel would always yare, fear, stand in awe of, their God.
basic.typology: The memorial stones that call God's people to remember His saving act point forward to the memorials God gives the church, above all the Lord's Supper, given so that we would remember and proclaim the greater deliverance won at the cross. The crossing they commemorate, a passage from wilderness to inheritance, pictures salvation in Christ.
basic.christ: The stones preserve the memory of a rescue through the waters, pointing to the far greater rescue accomplished by Jesus. As Israel was told to remember and retell the crossing, so Christ gives His people the bread and cup and says, do this in remembrance of Me, so that the mighty saving hand of God at the cross would be proclaimed until He comes.
basic.god: God is the God who acts mightily and who wants His acts known. He dried up the Jordan as He dried up the Red Sea, showing His unchanging power across the generations. He works so that all the peoples of the earth would know His hand, and so that His people would live in reverent fear of Him. He is a God concerned not only to save but to be remembered and worshiped.
basic.crossReferences: Exodus 12 gives the Passover as a memorial to be explained to children. Psalm 78 urges telling the coming generation the praises of the LORD. Deuteronomy 6 commands teaching God's works to one's children. And 1 Corinthians 11 records the Lord's Supper as the church's memorial of Christ.
basic.oneStory: God turns the crossing into a lasting memory so His mighty acts will be retold forever. The twelve stones join the long line of God-given reminders, from Passover to the Lord's Supper, by which each generation learns what God has done. They point to the greater deliverance in Christ, which His people are likewise called to remember and proclaim.

context.literary:
The chapter is framed by an identical question asked twice in almost the same words, what do these stones mean to you, verses 6 and 21, once given prospectively as an instruction to Joshua and once retrospectively as Joshua's own teaching to the people; the repetition is not clumsy doubling but a deliberate refrain that turns the whole chapter into an extended answer to a single catechetical question. Between the two occurrences of the question sits the actual crossing, verses 9 to 18, so that the narrative itself becomes the content of the answer a father will one day give his son.

The phrase to this day, verse 9, is the author's own signature, a formula scattered through Joshua and Judges, Joshua 4:9, 5:9, and 7:26, marking the gap between the event narrated and the time of writing, and quietly telling the first readers that the stones this chapter describes were not legend but a landmark still visible to them. The chapter's pacing also slows to a near standstill at its center, verses 10 to 13, repeating details of the crossing already given in chapter 3, priests standing, people hurrying across, the armed tribes going ahead, as though the narrator cannot move on until the completed crossing has been described a second time, in full, from the perspective of memory rather than instruction. The technique mirrors its own subject: a story about the deliberate slowing down of memory is itself deliberately slowed down in the telling.
context.historical:
Gilgal was not a single unique place name only here; several Gilgals appear elsewhere in the Old Testament, Deuteronomy 11:30 and 2 Kings 4:38 among them, which fits a word that most naturally functions as a common description, a circle, before it becomes fixed to any one location, exactly the kind of name a circle of standing stones would earn on the ground. This particular Gilgal, on the plains near Jericho, becomes far more than a first campsite: Samuel later includes it in his yearly circuit of judging Israel, 1 Samuel 7:16, and Israel confirms Saul's kingship there before the LORD, 1 Samuel 11:14 to 15, so that the site where Israel first remembered its entrance into the land keeps functioning, generations later, as a place where the nation renews its relationship to God and to His anointed leader.

Standing stones set up to mark an event, a boundary, or a covenant were a recognized practice across the ancient Near East, and Israel's own earlier history already includes them, Jacob's pillar at Bethel, Genesis 28:18, and the stone he and Laban raise as a covenant witness, Genesis 31:45 to 48. What is unusual here is the number and the source: twelve stones, one per tribe, taken not from a quarry or a hillside but from the exact place in the riverbed where the priests' feet stood, so the monument is not merely commemorative in a general sense but physically continuous with the miracle it explains.
context.canonical:
The twelve stones join a wider pattern of tribal stonework that runs through the whole Bible. At Sinai, Moses builds an altar and twelve pillars, one for each tribe, to seal the first covenant ceremony, Exodus 24:4. The high priest carries the names of the twelve tribes into the LORD's presence on twelve stones set in his breastpiece, one for each tribe by name, Exodus 28:21, so that Israel's worship is never represented by a single figure alone but by the whole covenant community named in stone before God. Centuries later, on Mount Carmel, Elijah repairs a broken altar of the LORD using twelve stones, according to the number of the tribes of the sons of Jacob, 1 Kings 18:31, deliberately reaching back to this same numerical grammar at the exact moment he calls a divided, idol worshiping people back to its covenant identity.

The pattern reaches its final form in Revelation's vision of the new Jerusalem, a city with twelve gates named for the twelve tribes of Israel and twelve foundations named for the twelve apostles of the Lamb, Revelation 21:12 to 14. What begins at the Jordan as an improvised monument from riverbed stones becomes the architecture of the eternal city itself: the whole people of God, from every stage of the story, built permanently into the place where God dwells with His people forever. The twelve stones at Gilgal are a small, provisional version of a much larger truth, that God numbers, names, and keeps every tribe of His people in lasting, visible form.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The author gives the instructions for the memorial before the crossing is even finished, verses 1 to 8, rather than adding them afterward as an editorial reflection; meaning is fixed in place before memory has any chance to drift or embellish. That order matters, because the author writing this book already knows how the story of this generation ends: Judges 2:10 records that after Joshua's generation died, another generation arose who did not know the LORD or the work He had done for Israel.

The stones at Gilgal are the author's own answer, given in advance, to a failure he is not hiding from his readers; he wants Israel, reading this account later, to see exactly where a safeguard against forgetting had been built into their history and to ask themselves whether they, unlike their fathers, will use it. The double telling of the child's question, once as command and once as fulfilled teaching, verses 6 to 7 and 21 to 23, is meant to be rehearsed, not merely read, an intended liturgy for the home as much as a report for the record, so that every future generation's ignorance of the LORD would be inexcusable rather than inevitable.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Nothing in the chapter instructs later believers to build stone monuments at significant moments in their own lives, and nothing suggests the stones themselves carried any power; they are described purely as prompts to a story, never as objects to be venerated, prayed to, or visited as pilgrimage relics, an important guard against turning this account into justification for a general theology of sacred objects.

What does transfer directly is the method modeled twice in the chapter: build something, whether a stone, a habit, a family tradition, that will provoke a child's honest question, and be ready to answer that question with the actual story of what God has done, not a vague sentiment. Deuteronomy commands the same pattern in words rather than stone, when your son asks, tell him, Deuteronomy 6:20 to 21, showing that the enduring command is the teaching itself, in whatever form makes the question arise.

debates.question: Were there two sets of stones, one at Gilgal and one left in the riverbed?

views.label: Two distinct memorials
views.case: The plain reading of verses 8 and 20 has twelve stones carried out and set up at Gilgal, while verse 9 says Joshua also set up twelve stones in the middle of the Jordan where the priests stood; two memorials, one visible on land and one marking the exact spot of the miracle, each testifying to the same event.

views.label: One memorial, with verse 9 clarified by the footnote
views.case: Some translators render verse 9 as Joshua set up the twelve stones that had been in the middle of the Jordan, as the BSB footnote notes, understanding a single set of stones taken from the river and erected at Gilgal, so the chapter describes one memorial from different angles.

debates.bearing: Either way the point stands: the crossing is deliberately marked with stone so that its memory endures; the number twelve, one per tribe, binds the whole nation to the testimony.

debates.question: Is the number about 40,000 armed men, verse 13, meant as an exact headcount?

views.label: A real, if rounded, number of troops
views.case: The text reads as straightforward military reporting, and many interpreters take the 40,000 as an approximate but genuine count of the fighting men from the two and a half tribes who had committed to cross armed ahead of the rest, consistent with the sworn commitment those tribes made to Moses, Numbers 32:20 to 22.

views.label: A round number using a flexible military term
views.case: Others note that the Hebrew word often rendered thousand, eleph, can also denote a military unit, clan, or contingent smaller than a literal thousand elsewhere in the Old Testament, and that round, formulaic numbers were a common way ancient Near Eastern texts reported army sizes for effect rather than for a precise census.

debates.bearing: Either reading leaves the chapter's own point untouched: a substantial, organized force from Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh kept its promise and crossed armed for battle before the LORD, in full view of the rest of the nation, verse 12.

study.originalLanguages:
Beyond zikkaron, yad, and yare, several other words color the chapter's vocabulary of memory. The whole account is framed by a stock Hebrew formula, ad hayyom hazeh, to this day, verse 9, a phrase the author of Joshua reaches for repeatedly, 5:9, 7:26, and 9:27, always to tell readers that what they are being told left a mark still visible when the book was written; it functions almost like a historian's footnote embedded directly in the narrative voice.

The verb behind carried in take up for yourselves twelve stones and carry them, verses 3 and 5, is nasa, one of the most flexible verbs in Biblical Hebrew, covering everything from lifting a physical load to bearing responsibility to, in its most theologically loaded sense, forgiving or carrying away guilt, as when the LORD is described as forgiving, literally bearing away, iniquity and transgression and sin, Exodus 34:7. The twelve men nasa stones out of the river on their shoulders; the same verb elsewhere describes God bearing away the very guilt that the flood of judgment, pictured everywhere else in Scripture as overwhelming water, would otherwise have exacted. The stones are lifted, and in a sense so is a burden of memory that could otherwise have sunk without a physical marker to carry it.

Twice the text uses forms of qum, to rise, stand, or be established, for the setting up of the stones, verses 9 and 20, the same root that describes a covenant being established, a king being raised up, or a word being confirmed and made to stand. Choosing qum rather than a simple verb for placing an object treats the stones less like furniture and more like a standing, ongoing testimony, something raised up to remain upright as long as Israel remains a nation, exactly as long as the crossing itself needs to be believed.

One further word deserves note: the stones are said to serve as an oth, a sign, among you, verse 6, the same word used of the rainbow after the flood, Genesis 9:12 to 13, and of the blood on Egypt's doorposts, Exodus 12:13. Israel's history is marked again and again by divinely appointed signs, physical, visible, and pointing beyond themselves to a specific saving act; the twelve stones take their place in that same line of signs, joining rainbow and blood and every other sign Scripture records as evidence that this God has always preferred to leave His people something they can see and touch, not only something they must simply take on faith.

typology.type: The memorial stones that preserve and retell a saving act
typology.fulfillment: Israel is told to explain the stones by retelling a specific historical claim: the waters of the Jordan were cut off before the ark of the covenant, verse 7, not a vague sentiment about God's goodness but a datable, particular saving act. The Lord's Supper works the same way: this is My body, this is My blood of the covenant, 1 Corinthians 11:24 to 25, is likewise an unrepeatable historical act commemorated in a repeatable physical sign, bread and cup standing in for stones, so that every future generation of the church answers its own child's question, what does this mean, with an equally specific, historical gospel rather than a general religious feeling. The type is imperfect since stones can only prompt a question and point away from themselves to a story, while the Supper both points to Christ's death and, Paul says, actually proclaims it, shaping the participants who eat and drink.

typology.type: The crossing of the waters into the inheritance, remembered forever
typology.fulfillment: Israel's crossing into the land completes a rescue that began at the Red Sea, one people passing through water twice, at the start and the end of the same journey, into an inheritance neither crossing could have produced alone. Paul reads the whole sequence, cloud, sea, manna, water from the rock, as written for our instruction, on whom the fulfillment of the ages has come, 1 Corinthians 10:1 to 4 and 10:11, treating Israel's water crossings as a pattern completed in the greater exodus Christ accomplishes for His people, a rescue from slavery to sin into an inheritance that, unlike Canaan, cannot be lost, 1 Peter 1:4. The type is not identical, since Israel's inheritance still had to be fought for tribe by tribe after the crossing, while the inheritance kept for believers is already imperishable and undefiled before they ever arrive.

typology.type: The child's question answered by the story of God's deliverance
typology.fulfillment: The whole chapter assumes that faith is never automatically inherited; each generation must be told the story and choose to believe it for themselves, which is exactly the New Testament's own concern for handing on sound teaching. Paul reminds Timothy of the sincere faith that first lived in his grandmother Lois and mother Eunice, and I am persuaded, lives in you as well, 2 Timothy 1:5, and Jude urges his readers to contend earnestly for the faith that was once for all delivered to the saints, Jude 3, treating the gospel itself as a kind of memorial handed carefully from one generation to the next. The type is loose rather than exact, since the stones needed only to prompt a question that could be answered with a fixed, unchanging story, while the church's faith must also be actively defended against those who would alter or deny the story it hands on.

typology.type: Stones taken from the exact place where the miracle happened and built into a lasting structure, Joshua 4:3 and 4:9
typology.fulfillment: These stones are not generic building material; they are identified specifically as the ones that stood where the priests' feet stood in the middle of the miracle itself, so the structure they form is inseparable from the saving event it commemorates. Peter describes believers coming to Christ, a living stone rejected by men but chosen and precious by God, and being built themselves into a spiritual house, 1 Peter 2:4 to 5, with Christ Himself as the cornerstone chosen and precious, 1 Peter 2:6. The twelve stones from the Jordan, taken up and built into one monument, foreshadow a people taken out of the very place of death and judgment and built together into God's own dwelling. The type is imperfect because the Gilgal stones remain inert markers of a past event, while the living stones Peter describes are themselves alive, continually being built and growing into the structure they belong to.

study.christ:
Verse 1 notes something easy to miss: the whole nation had finished crossing before God gives the command about the stones, and verse 11 repeats that after everyone had finished crossing the priests came up. Nobody is left behind in the current, no household forgotten in the strong flow, none too slow or too weak to make it across; the completed, comprehensive nature of the crossing anticipates a completed, comprehensive salvation. Jesus tells His Father that of all whom the Father gave Him He has lost none, John 6:39, and the good shepherd who leads sheep through danger brings the whole flock, not merely the strong ones, out safely, John 10:27 to 28. The memorial stones exist because the crossing they commemorate really was total: a picture of a redemption in which Christ, the true ark bearing God's presence through the flood, does not leave a single one of His own stranded in the current.

The chapter also closes the loop on Joshua's exaltation, begun in chapter 3: they revered him all the days of his life, just as they had revered Moses, verse 14, language of settled, lasting honor rather than a passing moment of awe. Even that permanence has a limit built into it, since Joshua, like Moses, eventually dies, Joshua 24:29, and Israel's history after him keeps needing new leaders, better and worse, right down to the last king before exile. The writer of Hebrews contrasts every such leader, however honored, with a priest who continues forever because He holds His priesthood permanently, since He always lives to make intercession, Hebrews 7:24 to 25. Joshua is revered all his days, a phrase with an ending; Christ's honor and intercession have no such limit written into the promise.

Even the twelve stones point, in their number, toward Christ's own completed work among a whole people: twelve tribes, twelve stones, one testimony shared by the entire nation rather than kept by a favored few, foreshadowing the twelve apostles sent to gather a people from every tribe and tongue into the one testimony of what God has done in Christ, Matthew 19:28 and Revelation 21:14.
study.god:
Royal monuments across the ancient Near East, kings' inscriptions carved to celebrate their own victories and glorify their own names, were common enough that Israel's first monument on entering the land stands out by everything it refuses to do. No king's name is carved on these stones, no boast of strength is recorded, only a story that gives credit entirely to what the LORD did and nothing to what Israel achieved; the theology of the whole passage is compressed into what is left off the stones as much as what is written about them. This is a God who is jealous for His own reputation, verse 24, but entirely unconcerned to share that reputation with any human general or king, even one as honored as Joshua himself.

He is also a God who chooses plain materials for enduring purposes. The stones are not quarried, carved, or inscribed; they are simply lifted, as they were, from a riverbed, and their entire meaning depends on where they came from rather than on any craftsmanship applied to them afterward. That preference for plain, ready to hand materials, twelve stones instead of an engraved obelisk, matches a pattern across Scripture where God repeatedly builds significance into ordinary things, a rainbow, a jar of manna, a widow's flour, rather than requiring elaborate human artistry to carry His meaning.

And He is patient with an entire nation's memory in a way individual Israelites were not always patient with each other; the text assumes some children will ask honestly and some parents will need the stones there specifically to answer well, planning for spiritual forgetfulness generations in advance rather than assuming this generation's faith would simply transmit itself. He is, in other words, a God who plans for generations He will never audibly speak to directly, trusting ordinary parents to carry a story faithfully rather than sending a fresh miracle to every unbelieving heart that arises. That is a God who does not merely reveal Himself once and expect belief to be self sustaining; He builds structures, physical and liturgical, into the fabric of ordinary family life, expecting to be asked about and expecting to be explained, long after the original eyewitnesses of the miracle have died.

crossReferences.note: The Passover is given as a memorial to be explained to children when they ask its meaning, the same pattern of question and testimony that shapes the twelve stones at Gilgal.

When your son asks the meaning of God's commands, tell him the story of redemption, that we were slaves in Egypt and the LORD brought us out; faith is handed down by testimony, the exact instinct this chapter builds into stone.
Tell the coming generation the praises and works of the LORD, that they would set their hope in God and not forget His works, the same purpose the stones at Gilgal were raised to serve.

The Lord's Supper, the church's own memorial, is given so that Christ's saving death would be remembered and proclaimed until He comes, the New Testament counterpart to a stone monument by the Jordan.
The Jordan crossing is bound explicitly to the Red Sea, framing Israel's whole journey between two deliberate partings of the waters, both worked by the same God's hand a generation apart.
At Sinai, Moses builds an altar and sets up twelve pillars for the twelve tribes to seal the first covenant, the same numerical pattern repeated here at the Jordan for a second great covenant moment.

Elijah later rebuilds a ruined altar of twelve stones, according to the number of the tribes of the sons of Jacob, deliberately using the same tribal count to call a divided Israel back to the covenant this monument first marked.

A generation after Joshua arises that does not know the LORD or what He had done for Israel, the very failure of memory this chapter's monument was built to prevent, showing how urgently needed such reminders can be.

Believers are living stones built into a spiritual house on the cornerstone of Christ, an image that echoes the twelve stones taken from the place of the miracle and built into one lasting testimony at Gilgal.

study.oneStory:
Memory runs all through the Bible's story as both a gift and an obligation. The stones at Gilgal are one piece of a much larger habit God builds into Israel from the beginning, feast days tied to specific events, Passover to the exodus, Sukkot to the wilderness, this monument to the crossing, so that Israel's whole calendar becomes a structure for not forgetting. The purpose named twice in this chapter, that Israel would fear the LORD and that the nations would know His mighty hand, sets the terms for everything that follows: a people who remember rightly worship rightly, and a people who forget, as Judges soon reports they did, drift quickly into worshiping whatever god happens to be nearest.

Yet Scripture also promises a strange and merciful kind of forgetting alongside all this remembering. The LORD tells Jeremiah that under the new covenant He will forgive iniquity and remember sin no more, Jeremiah 31:34, and Isaiah promises a new heavens and a new earth in which the former troubles will not even come to mind, Isaiah 65:17. The two movements are not contradictory; they are precisely calibrated. What must never be forgotten is what God has done to save; what must finally be forgotten, and only God can accomplish this, is the sin and suffering that saving work overcame. The twelve stones exist so grace is never forgotten. The new creation exists so guilt and grief finally will be.

That is where this small monument at Gilgal is quietly heading. It stands at the very start of Israel's life in the land as a promise that God's mighty acts will be told and retold, generation after generation, until the story running from the exodus, through the Jordan, through the greater deliverance at the cross, arrives at a city where the redeemed no longer need a stone to remember, because they stand in the very presence of the One the stones were always pointing to, and every former thing that needed remembering in order to be overcome has, at last, been forgotten for good.

quiz.q: Why did God command Israel to set up the twelve stones?

options.text: As a memorial, so that future generations would ask their meaning and be told what God had done.
options.note: Verses 6 to 7 and 21 to 23 make teaching the next generation the stated purpose.

options.text: As an altar for offering sacrifices to the LORD.
options.note: Stones were sometimes used for altars, but these were specifically a memorial to prompt remembrance, not an altar.

options.text: As a boundary marker for the tribe of Judah's land.
options.note: They marked no tribal boundary; they were a national memorial of the crossing.

options.text: As a defensive wall against Jericho.
options.note: They had no military purpose; they were a teaching memorial.

quiz.q: How many stones were taken, and why that number?

options.text: Twelve, one for each tribe of Israel, so the whole nation shared in the testimony.
options.note: Verses 2 to 8 tie the twelve stones to the twelve tribes, binding all Israel to the memory.

options.text: Twelve, one for each of Joshua's chief officers.
options.note: The number twelve is right, but it represents the tribes of Israel, not Joshua's officers.

options.text: Seven, matching the seven nations of Canaan.
options.note: There were twelve stones for the tribes, not seven for the nations.

options.text: A random pile with no particular number.
options.note: The number was deliberate: twelve, one per tribe.

quiz.q: What twofold purpose did God give for the whole event?

options.text: That all the earth would know His hand is mighty, and that Israel would always fear Him.
That Israel would grow wealthy and that their enemies would flee.
options.note: God did give victory, but the stated purpose was knowledge of His might and the fear of Him, not wealth.

options.text: That Joshua would be crowned king over Israel.
options.note: Joshua was exalted as leader, but the purpose given is God's glory and Israel's reverence, not a coronation.

options.text: That the memory of Moses would be erased.
options.note: Israel revered Joshua as they had revered Moses; nothing here erases Moses.

quiz.q: How does the memorial of stones point forward in Scripture?

options.text: To the memorials God gives His people to remember His saving acts, above all the Lord's Supper.
options.note: Remembering and retelling God's deliverance runs from Passover to the Lord's Supper, 1 Corinthians 11:24-26.

options.text: To the idea that God's works are best forgotten over time.
options.note: The opposite: the whole point is that God's works be remembered and retold, not forgotten.

options.text: To a command that every generation build its own stone pile.
options.note: The lasting principle is remembrance and teaching, not reproducing this specific monument.

options.text: To nothing beyond ancient Israel's history.
options.note: The pattern of God-given memorials continues to the church's remembrance of Christ.

questions: God built a reminder so His acts would not be forgotten. What practices or markers help you remember what God has done in your life, and where might you need more of them?
The stones existed to answer a child's question with the story of God's power. How are you passing on the story of what God has done to those coming after you?
God dried up the Jordan just as He had the Red Sea, showing His power is the same across generations. Where do you need to trust that the God who acted before will act again?
The purpose of remembering was that Israel would always fear the LORD. How does recalling God's mighty acts stir up reverent awe and trust in you today?
The Lord's Supper is the church's memorial of a greater crossing, the deliverance won at the cross. How can you come to it, or to any remembrance of Christ, with fresh wonder at God's saving hand?

translationNotes.note: The BSB footnote notes that some translators render this as Joshua set up the twelve stones that had been in the middle of the Jordan, which bears on whether there were one or two sets of stones.
The ark of the Testimony is another name for the ark of the covenant, as the BSB footnote notes; the Testimony refers to the covenant tablets it contained.
The tenth day of the first month is the day the Passover lamb was to be chosen, Exodus 12:3, linking the entry into the land to the exodus deliverance.
